145-r1.sourceTitle: Abelian Varieties (v2.00), J. S. Milne, Ch. II §1 and Ch. III §11
145-r1.locator: Chapter II, §1, Theorem 1.1 and proof (pp. 75-76); Chapter III, §11, Theorem 11.1 and Proposition 11.2 (pp. 117-118)
145-r1.proofSketch: For an abelian variety $A$ over $\mathbb F_q$, the Frobenius endomorphism $\pi$ satisfies $|A(\mathbb F_{q^m})|=\prod(1-a_i^m)$, where $a_i$ are the eigenvalues of $\pi$ on $T_\ell A$: $\pi-1$ is étale, so its kernel $A(\mathbb F_q)$ has size $\deg(\pi-1)=P_\pi(1)$. The Rosati involution attached to a polarization satisfies $\pi^\dagger\pi=q$ (Lemma 1.2), and a positivity argument in the semisimple algebra $\mathbb Q[\pi]$ (Lemma 1.3) then gives $|a_i|=q^{1/2}$. For a curve $C$ with Jacobian $J$, the Lefschetz-type formula $(\Gamma_\alpha\cdot\Delta)=1-\mathrm{Tr}(\alpha')+\deg\alpha$ (Prop. 11.2) applied to the Frobenius of $C$ shows $N=1-\sum a_i+q$ for the eigenvalues $a_i$ of $\pi_J$. Since $|a_i|=q^{1/2}$ there are $2g$ of them, so $|N-q-1|\le 2g\,q^{1/2}$.

145-r1.transcriptionNotes: Excerpt shows the statement and main steps; Lemma 1.3 (p. 77-78, positivity argument for the Rosati involution) and the proof of Proposition 11.2 (pp. 118-119) are not reproduced.

145-r2.sourceTitle: The Riemann Hypothesis over Finite Fields: From Weil to the Present Day, J. S. Milne, §1 (Weil's work in the 1940s and 1950s)
145-r2.locator: arXiv:1509.00797v1, Section 1, subsection 'The inequality of Castelnuovo-Severi' through 'Proof of the Riemann hypothesis for curves', Thm 1.5, Cor 1.6, Example 1.7 (pp. 9-10)
145-r2.proofSketch: On $V=C_1\times C_2$ one has $C_1^2=C_2^2=0$, $C_1\cdot C_2=1$. For a divisor $D$ with $d_1=D\cdot C_1$, $d_2=D\cdot C_2$, the class $D-d_2C_1-d_1C_2$ is orthogonal to the ample-type class $C_1+C_2$ (self-intersection $2>0$), so the Hodge index theorem gives $(D-d_2C_1-d_1C_2)^2\le0$, i.e. $D^2\le 2d_1d_2$. Defining the defect $\mathrm{def}(D)=2d_1d_2-D^2\ge0$, positivity of $\mathrm{def}(mD+nD')$ in $m,n$ yields $|D\cdot D'-d_1d_2'-d_2d_1'|\le(\mathrm{def}D\,\mathrm{def}D')^{1/2}$. For a morphism $f$ the adjunction formula gives $\mathrm{def}(\Gamma_f)=2g_2\deg f$. Applying this to the diagonal ($\mathrm{def}=2g$) and the Frobenius graph ($\mathrm{def}=2gq$) on $C\times C$ gives $|(\Delta\cdot\Gamma_\pi)-q-1|\le 2gq^{1/2}$, and $(\Delta\cdot\Gamma_\pi)$ is the number of rational points.

images.caption: Milne, Riemann Hypothesis over Finite Fields, p. 9: setup on C1 x C2, Theorem 1.5 (Castelnuovo-Severi inequality) via Hodge index theorem, equivalence defect, Corollary 1.6
p. 10: proof of Cor. 1.6, Example 1.7 (def of a graph by adjunction), and the proof of the Riemann hypothesis for curves

145-r2.attribution: James S. Milne, The Riemann Hypothesis over Finite Fields: From Weil to the Present Day, arXiv:1509.00797 (2015).
145-r2.transcriptionNotes: Takes the Hodge index theorem (Thm 1.2) as input, stated on the preceding page and not reproduced. This is Weil's 1941 proof as simplified via Hodge index / Mattuck-Tate / Grothendieck; Weil's original (without Riemann-Roch on the surface) is only sketched later in the same section.

145-r3.sourceTitle: The Bombieri-Stepanov proof of the Hasse-Weil bound, Terence Tao (What's new blog, 2 May 2014)
145-r3.locator: Blog post body: Theorem 2 (weak Hasse-Weil bound), eqs. (2)-(12), Lemma 3, Proposition 4; Theorem 1 deduced in the remaining sections
145-r3.proofSketch: Assuming $q$ is a perfect square, $|C(\mathbb F_q)|$ is the number of intersection points of $C_1=\{(z,\mathrm{Frob}_{\sqrt q}z)\}$ and its transpose $C_2$ on $C\times C$. Choose a rational point $P_\infty$ and let $R_n$ be the functions on $C$ with a pole of order at most $n$ only at $P_\infty$; Riemann's inequality gives $\dim R_n\ge n+1-g$. Take $V=R_\ell\otimes R_m\subset k(C\times C)$, of dimension at least $(\ell+1-g)(m+1-g)$. Its restriction to $C_1$ has dimension at most $\ell+m\sqrt q+1$ and to $C_2$ at most $\ell\sqrt q+m+1$; for $m$ slightly larger than $\ell$ the second restriction map is not injective. If $\ell<\sqrt q$ the first restriction is injective (distinct pole orders at $P_\infty$), so a nonzero $f\in V$ vanishes on $C_2$ but not on $C_1$. Its restriction to $C_1$ vanishes on $C_1\cap C_2$, which has $|C(\mathbb F_q)|$ points, and has at most $\ell+m\sqrt q$ poles. Hence $|C(\mathbb F_q)|\le\ell+m\sqrt q$; the choice $m=\sqrt q+2g$, $\ell\approx\frac{g}{g+1}\sqrt q+g+1$ gives the weak bound.

145-r3.attribution: Terence Tao, 'The Bombieri-Stepanov proof of the Hasse-Weil bound', What's new, 2 May 2014.
145-r3.transcriptionNotes: The page shows the weak bound (q a square, q >= (g+1)^4); the passage to the full Hasse-Weil bound (lower bound via Galois covers, tensor power trick) in the later sections of the post is not reproduced. Screenshots of the post body cropped from the right column.

145-r4.sourceTitle: The Weil Conjecture. I, Pierre Deligne (English translation of 'La conjecture de Weil. I', hosted by J. S. Milne), §1 and §3
145-r4.locator: Theorem (1.6), Lemma (1.7) and proof of (1.7)=>(1.6); §3 'The main lemma', Theorem (3.2) and its proof (pp. 4-12 of the PDF)
145-r4.proofSketch: Grothendieck's trace formula expresses $Z(X_0,t)$ through $\det(1-F^*t,H^i_c)$. Theorem 1.6 (weights are $q^{i/2}$) is reduced to Lemma 1.7 (eigenvalues have complex conjugates of absolute value $q^{i/2}$): rationality and a Hankel-determinant/Fatou argument show the polynomials $P_i$ are rational with integer coefficients and independent of $\ell$. The key estimate (Theorem 3.2, inspired by Rankin) takes a sheaf with a symplectic form whose monodromy is open in $\mathrm{Sp}$ and shows it is pure: for the $2k$-th tensor power, the local factors have positive coefficients, and its $L$-function has only the pole $1/q^{k\beta+1}$ by invariant theory, so Rankin's positivity lemma bounds $|\alpha|\le q_x^{\beta/2+1/(2k)}$; letting $k\to\infty$ and using the symplectic duality gives $|\alpha|=q_x^{\beta/2}$. Lefschetz pencils later supply the needed monodromy hypothesis.
